options: A primitive addition instruction with no method involved
`type(a).__add__(a, b)`, with a fallback to `type(b).__radd__(b, a)`
why: Every operator is a method call the type can implement, which is why your own classes can take part in the same syntax as the built-in ones.

q: Where does Python look up a dunder for an implicit call like `len(x)`?
options: On the instance, then the type
On the module the class was defined in
why: Which is why assigning `obj.__len__ = f` does not change what `len(obj)` does, and why `hasattr(x, "__call__")` is unreliable.

q: If you implement only one of `__str__` and `__repr__`, which should it be?
options: Neither is more useful than the other
why: `str()` falls back to `__repr__`, so one method covers both. The reverse fallback does not exist.
A container's own repr renders its elements with `repr`, which is why an object with only `__str__` is unreadable inside a list.

q: An object whose class defines neither `__bool__` nor `__len__` is
options: True only if it has attributes
An error in a boolean context
why: The default is truthy, which is why a class representing something empty is true unless you say otherwise.
Implementing `__len__` therefore gives you both `len(x)` and correct truthiness from a single method.

q: Defining `__eq__` on a class does what to `__hash__`?
options: Sets it to `None`, making instances unhashable
why: A hash table compares for equality inside a bucket, so equal objects must hash equal. Python withdraws hashing rather than let you build that bug.

q: Your `__add__` is handed a type it cannot add. What should it do?
why: Returning `NotImplemented` lets Python try the other operand's `__radd__` and, if that also declines, raise a better error than you would have written.

options: Two names for the same thing
A value you return and an exception you raise, meaning different things
why: `NotImplemented` means "I decline this operand, try someone else". `NotImplementedError` means "this abstract method needs overriding".

q: `x in obj` when the class has neither `__contains__` nor `__iter__`
options: Raises TypeError saying the object is not iterable
why: `in` falls back from `__contains__` to iteration, and the error names the fallback rather than the first choice.

options: Returns the length of the string
why: Several dunder contracts are enforced by the interpreter rather than trusted: `__len__` must give a non-negative integer, `__bool__` a bool, `__hash__` an integer.

q: `type(x) is C` differs from `isinstance(x, C)` in that
options: `type(x) is C` rejects subclasses of C
They are identical for user-defined classes
why: Rejecting subclasses defeats the point of having them, so `isinstance` is nearly always the one you want.

q: Why does an `isinstance(x, int)` branch need care when booleans are involved?
options: `bool` is a subclass of `int`, so that branch catches `True` and `False` too
why: Put the `bool` branch first if the two need distinguishing.

q: Which of these is not an object in Python?
options: None of them; all three are objects
why: Functions, classes and modules are all ordinary objects, which is what makes decorators and dispatch tables possible.

q: Duck typing means Python decides what an object can do by
options: Whether it has the methods the operation needs
why: The cost is that the requirement is invisible to readers and checkers, which is what `typing.Protocol` exists to fix.
